newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir autonomy seen stiffening Indian federalism.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir autonomy seen stiffening Indian federalism.

text.p: Steps towards greater autonomy for India's northern Jammu and Kashmir state will gather speed after a new government takes office next week and will help to strengthen India's federal structure, analysts said on Sunday.
With a promise of regional autonomy, the moderate National Conference party last week swept the first local polls in the Himalayan region since a separatist revolt broke out in 1990.
Led by the charismatic Farooq Abdullah, it won 57 seats in the state's 87-member assembly, inflicting a crushing defeat on the other pro-Indian parties in the troubled state.

"Autonomy for the three regions, we shall implement within a year," said Abdullah, 60, who will lead the state's first elected government in nearly seven years, at a news conference on Saturday in the summer capital of Srinagar.
The state covers the mainly Moslem Kashmir Valley, the focus of a separatist rebellion, Jammu, which is mostly inhabited by Hindus, and the Buddhist-dominated Ladakh region.
Political commentators feel the demand for more autonomy could evoke similar sentiments in some of India's 25 other states, which could translate into a stronger federal structure.

"Kashmir will be an important staging-post in the evolution of Indian unity," M.J. Akbar, editor of the Asian Age newspaper, told Reuters. "Every part of India wants to be represented at the centre by people who genuinely represent it."
For many years, a strong central government in New Delhi has dominated India's federalist structure, Akbar said. But now the power of the federal government is waning.

Analysts said the strength of India's regional parties has grown as the country's oldest party, the Congress -- which has ruled for all but four years since independence -- has slowly decayed. Regional parties have become more and more assertive.
Riven by dissent and dogged by corruption, Congress suffered its worst-ever election defeat in May. Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 13-party United Front coalition replaced it.
Abdullah's party has joined Deve Gowda's shaky coalition.
"Kashmir is a microcosm of modernist India," said Rasheed Talib, another political commentator. "It is a pointer to the fact that India must move towards federalism."

The Indian constitution leaves all Kashmiri affairs in local hands except for foreign relations, communications and defence. Since 1952, the federal government in New Delhi has taken over this power, Kashmiris say. They look to Abdullah to reclaim it.

Abdullah's party, one seat short of a two-thirds majority, has the necessary numbers to push through its autonomy plans in the state's assembly. However, it will need the support of the federal government to implement them.
The Communist Party of India (Marxist), a Deve Gowda ally, favours full autonomy for the state. But main opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party has vowed to oppose such a move.
Abdullah's main task now is to bring peace to the rebellious region, where 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since 1990.

Abdullah said he was determined to negotiate with separatist leaders, who have refused an earlier offer to talk. "Even if they close their doors, I will break their doors and windows and open the way for negotiation," he said on Saturday.
Some analysts, however, feel Abdullah's immediate problems will be to deal with basic issues like safe drinking water, jobs and electricity.
A bloody seven-year rebellion has left the state with poor infrastructure, a dying tourist industry and a battered economy.
"He should set a time limit of about six months to deal with the nuts and bolts," said Kashmiri political scientist Amitabh Mattoo.
